forces: Two treble instruments and continuo; here violin, flute, viola da gamba and keyboard
performers: New Comma Baroque: Matthew C. Cataldi, Baroque violin; Leighann Daihl, Baroque flute; Phillip W. Serna, viola da gamba; Emily J. Morlan, historical keyboards
intro: A violin and flute trade long notes, quick runs and graceful little airs in the sonata that opens La Piémontaise. New Comma Baroque plays it with viola da gamba and keyboard sharing the bass: four people make Couperin’s three-part conversation.

relations.label: The first air returns
relations.basis: Inside the paired airs, the opening major-mode material returns after the minor-mode contrast. This agrees with the air at 274 s and the return to major described by the listening note near 450 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.966, sustained 37 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 158 s (cache/form/couperin-nations-piemontaise.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Four players, three lines
cues.text: Violin and flute take the two upper parts; gamba and keyboard share the bass. In the opening Gravement, one upper voice often holds a note while the other moves. Trills decorate the long notes, and the bass has ornaments of its own.
cues.evidence: Couperin, La Piémontoise, Cmaj7 edition (2022), score pp. 1–2. Performers are identified in the recording’s Commons description. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Saint-Gervais organ bench
cues.text: Couperin’s father Charles, organist of Saint-Gervais in Paris, died in 1679 and left the boy fatherless, with the post held in reserve for him. The great Lalande filled the organ bench until François could take it himself, in 1685.
cues.evidence: Opéra Royal de Versailles, biography of Couperin: Charles’s death in 1679, François titular by survivance, Lalande’s interim. Larousse, Dictionnaire de la musique: François in the post from 1685. https://www.operaroyal-versailles.fr/genre-event/couperin/ and https://www.larousse.fr/encyclopedie/musdico/Fran%C3%A7ois_Couperin/167027

cues.title: The bass joins the conversation
cues.text: The Vivement gives the bass running semiquavers as well as the upper parts. A phrase can begin below the violin and flute, then rise into their conversation. The keyboard and gamba have plenty to say together.
cues.evidence: Score, first Vivement, bars 30 onwards, pp. 3–5. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An Italian name for Couperin
cues.text: In his 1726 preface, Couperin tells a story about his first sonata. He presents it as the work of an Italian composer, whose name is an anagram of his own. The audience welcomes it. Encouraged, he writes more sonatas under the same disguise.
cues.evidence: Couperin’s preface to Les Nations (1726), discussed by Brian Robins, 22 July 2019. https://earlymusicreview.com/francois-couperin-les-nations-1726/

cues.title: A royal chapel by competition
cues.text: In 1693 Couperin’s teacher Thomelin, organist of the royal chapel, died. Couperin won the competition for the post, serving the January quarter of each year, and stayed an organist of the royal chapel for the rest of his working life.
cues.evidence: Larousse, Dictionnaire de la musique: after Thomelin’s death in 1693 he won the royal chapel organist’s post “par concours” for the January quarter. https://www.larousse.fr/encyclopedie/musdico/Fran%C3%A7ois_Couperin/167027. Opéra Royal de Versailles gives the same appointment: https://www.operaroyal-versailles.fr/genre-event/couperin/

cues.title: The violin sings alone
cues.text: The first air is in G major and marked Gracieusement. The violin carries its opening phrase while the flute rests. The bass answers with small steps and ornaments; then the flute takes up the tune and the violin falls silent.
cues.evidence: Score, first Air, pp. 12–13: first dessus alone above the bass in bars 1–7, second dessus enters in bar 8. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four nations on the title pages
cues.text: The four ordres of Les Nations bear grand names: France, Spain, the Empire and Piedmont. Each opens with an Italian-style sonata, then turns to French dances. Here, after the sonata, the printed score continues with an allemande marked “nobly, and without slowness”.
cues.evidence: Collection and design: https://earlymusicreview.com/francois-couperin-les-nations-1726/. Allemande marking, ‘Noblement, et sans lenteur’, score p. 20: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf. English translation is literal.

cues.title: The mirror and the key
cues.text: In L’Art de toucher le clavecin (1716) Couperin puts a mirror on the music desk to cure a pupil’s grimaces. With small children he takes the key of the harpsichord home, so nothing is undone while he is away that took him three quarters of an hour to set right.
cues.evidence: Couperin, L’Art de toucher le clavecin (1716), opening instructions on grimaces, the mirror and “la clef de l’instrument” (Nicolas Sceaux’s transcription, p. 2–3): https://musebaroque.fr/archives/Partitions/Couperin_clavecin2.pdf

cues.title: Corelli beside Lully
cues.text: Couperin names both Corelli and Lully in his preface to Les Nations, “both of whose compositions I shall love as long as I live”. Italian sonatas and French dances share his book. He has no wish to give up either composer.
cues.evidence: Couperin, preface to Les Nations (1726), in the English translation quoted by Brian Robins. https://earlymusicreview.com/francois-couperin-les-nations-1726/

cues.title: Dotted notes above a held bass
cues.text: The later Gravement et marqué begins with a long C in the bass. The violin sets out a dotted figure; the flute enters with it a bar later. Their short and long notes pull against the bass’s unbroken sound.
cues.evidence: Score, Gravement et marqué, p. 16, opening three bars: held C in the bass and successive entries of the upper parts. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Six quavers, three moving parts
cues.text: The final Légèrement changes to six-eight. The flute begins the running quavers while the violin rests; soon the figures pass between the upper parts and the bass. The long sonata ends with all three lines still taking their turns.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass breaks into running notes
transitions.how: A D major chord closes the slow opening. Vivement begins in G minor and common time: the violin drops out after its first note while flute and bass keep moving. Running semiquavers soon pass between the gamba, keyboard and upper instruments. Couperin replaces the opening’s long overlaps with brisk exchanges.
transitions.evidence: Score, bars 29–33, p. 3: D major closing chord and Vivement in common time. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf

transitions.title: E♭ under the held notes
transitions.how: The new Gravement opens on E♭ major: E♭ in the bass, G and B♭ in the upper parts. The metre returns to three-two, and violin and flute hold long notes. Later Couperin asks for notes égales, evenly played notes, as the gamba and keyboard bass begin moving beneath them.

transitions.title: A graceful tune over G
transitions.to: E · Two airs and a return
transitions.how: The quick movement slows to très lentement and closes on D major. The air answers in G major, with G in the bass and a three-beat metre. Marked Gracieusement, the violin begins a rounded, ornamented phrase over gamba and keyboard; the flute rests before taking its turn.
transitions.evidence: Score, final bars of Vivement et marqué and opening of the Air, pp. 11–12. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf

transitions.title: From dotted notes to six-eight
transitions.how: The slow section reaches D major before Légèrement begins over G in the bass. Six-eight replaces common time. The flute starts a stream of quavers; the violin gives a single note, then rests. Gamba and keyboard keep dotted crotchets beneath the first phrase before joining the quicker movement.
transitions.evidence: Score, join between Gravement et marqué and Légèrement, p. 17. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/25/IMSLP779316-PMLP297657-Couperin_-_La_Pi%C3%A9montoise.pdf

composer.epithet: He played for Louis XIV on Sundays and taught the harpsichord to speak through a held note, a trill and a well-placed silence.
facts: Son of Charles Couperin; nephew of Louis; organist at Saint-Gervais from 1685
Royal chapel organist from 1693; chamber harpsichordist from 1717
Four books, 1713–30: 27 ordres; L’Art de toucher le clavecin, 1716–17
Two organ masses; Leçons de Ténèbres; chamber concerts and viol suites
composer.background:
On Sundays in 1714 and 1715, François Couperin played chamber music for the ageing Louis XIV. The violinist François Duval joined him, with wind players and a viol; Couperin sat at the harpsichord. When he published the Concerts royaux in 1722, he remembered the king summoning him “almost every Sunday of the year”. These dances had been tried out before a man who had once danced in his own court ballets. Now they came to him in his rooms: an allemande, a grave sarabande, a little chaconne.

Couperin was born in Paris in 1668, into a family already established at the organ of Saint-Gervais. His uncle Louis had held the post before his father Charles, and had died before François was born. When Charles died in 1679, the church kept the succession open for the boy; Michel-Richard de Lalande covered the duties until he was ready. François studied with Jacques Thomelin and took over in 1685. At twenty-five he won one of the four organists’ places at the royal chapel. He kept his Paris work, travelled to court for his quarter of service and taught the royal children.
